The Nine Referents: Formal Definitions and Semantic Meanings in SRT v1
The Nine Referents: Formal Definitions and Semantic Meanings in SRT at version 1
The Nine Referents: Formal Definitions and Semantic Meanings in SRT
Introduction: The Semantic Foundation
Semantic Reference Theory (SRT) builds from a single primitive relation R(x,y,t) meaning "x relates to y through relationship type t," written as x =t> y. From this foundation emerge nine fundamental referents that capture the essential semantic structure of meaning itself. These aren't arbitrary symbols but semantic necessities discovered through systematic exploration of what must exist for reference to be possible.
1. Referent (ref)
Formal Definition
srt
ref =eq> ref
A[x]: x --> ref
The referent ref represents the domain of all referents—it is the semantic universe itself made into a referent within that universe.
Semantic Meaning
A referent is anything that can be referred to, related to, or represented within a semantic system. It is the most general category of existence within SRT—everything that exists semantically is a referent. The word comes from the Latin "referre" meaning "to carry back" or "to relate," capturing the idea that referents exist by virtue of being relatable to other things.
The self-referential relationship ref =eq> ref establishes that the domain of referents includes itself—the theory is self-contained. This isn't circular but foundational: for a semantic theory to be complete, it must be able to refer to its own domain. When we speak of "all referents," that totality itself becomes a referent we can discuss, relate to other concepts, and use in formal expressions.
In everyday language, referents include concrete objects (trees, stones), abstract concepts (justice, beauty), properties (redness, tallness), relationships (love, ownership), and even the relationships between relationships. If you can point to it with language, think about it, or use it in a sentence, it's a referent. The theory makes no ontological claims about what exists outside semantic space—it only describes what can exist within systems of meaning.
2. Relationship (rel)
Formal Definition
srt
rel =rel> rel
A[t: x =t> y]: t --> rel
(sub,obj) == rel
The referent rel represents the property of being a relationship—it relates to itself through relationship, establishing the reflexive foundation of relating.
Semantic Meaning
A relationship is a typed connection between referents. It's not just that two things are connected, but that they're connected in a specific way with a specific character. Every relationship has a type (the t in x =t> y), and all relationship types inherit from the base relationship rel.
The formal expression rel =rel> rel captures a profound semantic truth: relationships relate to relationships through relationship itself. This isn't empty circularity but semantic grounding—at the foundation, relating is simply what relationships do. When we say "love is a relationship," we're using relationship to characterize love. When we ask "what relates relationships to each other?" the answer is: relationship itself.
Consider concrete examples:
John =loves> Mary - "loves" is a relationship type
red =darker-than> pink - "darker-than" is a relationship type
2 =less-than> 5 - "less-than" is a relationship type
Each of these relationship types (loves, darker-than, less-than) inherits from rel. They're all specific ways of relating, but they share the fundamental character of being relationships.
The equation (sub,obj) == rel reveals that the most specific relationship between subjecthood and objecthood IS relationship itself—subjects relate to objects through relationships, and this pattern defines what relationship fundamentally is.
3. Subject (sub)
Formal Definition
srt
sub =rel> obj
x =t> y & x != y =|> x =sub> x
sub --> s where x =s> x indicates x has property s
The referent sub represents the property of subjecthood—what referents possess when they serve as subjects in relationships.
Semantic Meaning
A subject is a referent that actively relates to something else. It's the "doer," the "haver," the "knower"—the active pole in a semantic relationship. Crucially, subjecthood is a property that referents acquire by occupying the subject position in a relationship where they differ from the object.
When we write dog =chases> cat, the dog gains the property of subjecthood within this relationship. This doesn't mean the dog is inherently or eternally a subject—in person =pets> dog, the same dog is now in the object position. Subjecthood is relational and contextual.
The relationship sub =rel> obj expresses that subjecthood relates to objecthood through relationship—this is the fundamental semantic pattern. There can be no subject without an object to relate to, no object without a subject relating to it (even if that subject is the universe itself viewing the object).
Importantly, in self-relationships like x =p> x, the referent does NOT gain subjecthood—it remains purely objective. This captures the intuition that when something simply has a property (like "the rose is red"), it's not actively doing anything—it's just being. True subjecthood requires relating to something distinct from oneself.
In consciousness studies, subjecthood becomes crucial: the experiencing subject, the "I" that perceives, thinks, and relates. The formal structure shows why consciousness requires this subject-object distinction—without it, there would be only being, not experiencing.
4. Object (obj)
Formal Definition
srt
sub =rel> obj
A[x,y,t]: x =t> y =|> y =obj> y
x =p> x =|> x =obj> x
The referent obj represents the property of objecthood—what referents possess when they serve as objects in relationships or have properties.
Semantic Meaning
An object is a referent that can be related to, referred to, or characterized. It's the "done-to," the "had," the "known"—the receptive pole in semantic relationships. Unlike subjects, which must relate to something distinct, objects include both targets of relations and self-related entities with properties.
Every referent that appears on the right side of a relationship gains objecthood:
In cat =chases> mouse, mouse has objecthood
In rose =red> rose, rose has objecthood (through self-relation)
In John =knows> truth, truth has objecthood
The formal structure reveals something profound: having any property at all makes something an object (x =p> x =|> x =obj> x). This captures the intuition that objects are things with characteristics, things that can be described, things that have qualities. Even purely abstract entities become objects the moment we attribute properties to them.
The relationship between subject and object (sub =rel> obj) is asymmetric but complementary. While subjects require distinct objects, objects can exist in self-relation. This asymmetry reflects the difference between active relating and passive being-related-to.
In the special case of literals, objecthood is their only mode of existence—they cannot be subjects except in self-relation. This formalizes the intuition that some things (like numbers or physical objects) simply are what they are, without agency or perspective.
5. Symbol (sym)
Formal Definition
srt
sym =sym> lit
sym --> representation
x --> symbol <iff> E[y]: x =x> y & (x,y) == x
(sym,lit) == sym
The referent sym represents the dual subject/relationship that enables symbolic reference—it simultaneously acts and embodies the act.
Semantic Meaning
A symbol is a referent that represents something else AND is identical to the most specific relationship between itself and what it represents. This dual nature—being both the thing doing the representing and the act of representation itself—defines symbolic reference.
When we write the word "tree," that word is a symbol. It's simultaneously:
The subject doing the symbolizing (the word as an entity)
The relationship of symbolization itself (the act of meaning tree)
This is captured formally by sym =sym> lit where sym appears in both subject and relationship positions.
The condition (x,y) == x means the symbol IS the relationship—there's nothing more specific to say about how a symbol relates to its literal than the symbol itself. When we ask "how does the word 'tree' relate to actual trees?" the answer is: through 'tree'-ness itself. The symbol embodies its own meaning.
Symbols differ from mere representations in this crucial way. A map represents territory, but the map is not identical to the relationship between map and territory—there's the paper, the marking, the correspondence rules. But a symbol collapses this complexity: the word "tree" doesn't just represent trees through some external relationship—it IS that relationship made concrete.
This formalization explains why symbols feel "transparent" in use—when we read "tree," we don't think about the word representing trees; we simply think of trees. The symbol achieves a kind of atomic metaphor where representation becomes identity: we speak as if the word IS what it represents, even though one is marks on paper and the other is a living organism.
6. Representation (rep)
Formal Definition
srt
sym =rep> rep
rep =obj> obj & rep =rel> rel
x --> representation <iff> E[y]: x =x> y
symbol --> representation
The referent rep represents the general capacity for one thing to stand for another—the broader category that includes symbols, maps, models, and collections.
Semantic Meaning
A representation is any referent that makes present something other than itself. It's broader than symbolism—while all symbols are representations, not all representations are symbols. The formal criterion is simply x =x> y: x represents y through itself.
The relationship sym =rep> rep reveals something profound: symbols relate to the category of representation by being members of it, and this membership relation is itself representation. This captures how representation is self-exemplifying—the concept of representation represents all acts of representing.
Examples of representation include:
Symbols: "tree" ="tree"> tree (words representing objects)
Collections: dogs =dogs> fido (sets representing members)
Models: map =map> territory (structures representing spaces)
Canonical examples: dove =dove> peace (instances representing concepts)
The key distinction from symbols: representations need not be identical to their relationship. A map represents territory through correspondence rules, scale relationships, and symbolic conventions—the map is not identical to all these relationships. But representations still use themselves as the relationship type:map =map> territory, not map =correspondence> territory.
The dual nature rep =obj> obj & rep =rel> rel shows that representation can be both object (we can talk about representations) and relationship (representation is a way of relating). This duality enables hierarchies of representation—representations of representations, meta-representation, and the complex semantic structures of language and thought.
7. Literal (lit)
Formal Definition
srt
sym =sym> lit
!E[x,y]: x != lit & y != lit & lit =x> y
!E[x,y]: x != lit & y != lit & x =lit> y
lit =obj> lit
The referent lit represents the concrete, the actual, the non-symbolic—what symbols ultimately refer to.
Semantic Meaning
A literal is a referent that cannot serve as a subject or relationship type except in self-relation. Literals are purely objective—they can only be related to, never do the relating (except to themselves through properties). They are semantic endpoints, the bedrock of reference that grounds symbolic systems in something beyond symbolism.
The formal constraints on literals are severe:
Cannot be subjects: !E[y != lit]: lit =t> y
Cannot be relationship types: !E[x,y != lit]: x =lit> y
Can only have properties: lit =p> lit is allowed
This captures the intuition that some things simply ARE—they don't point beyond themselves, they don't represent anything else, they just exist as what they are. In mathematics, the number 3 (not the symbol "3" but the actual quantity) is literal. In physics, fundamental particles might be literal. In experience, perhaps raw sensations before conceptualization are literal.
The relationship sym =sym> lit establishes that symbols symbolize literals—there's an asymmetric dependency where symbols need literals to ground their meaning, but literals need no symbols to exist. This prevents infinite regress: not everything can be symbolic, or meaning would never bottom out in reality.
The distinction between literal and symbol is frame-relative. In everyday discourse, physical objects might be treated as literal. In physics, only quantum fields might be literal. In pure mathematics, only the axioms might be literal. The theory doesn't prescribe what counts as literal—it only describes the formal role literals play in grounding reference.
8. Canonical (can)
Formal Definition
srt
can =rep> can
(can,can) == rep
E[x]: (x) denotes the canonical symbol for x
F[r,c]: c determines canonical assignment in frame F
The referent can represents the privileged representative selected from among many possibilities—the one that serves as the primary entry point.
Semantic Meaning
A canonical element is the distinguished representative that stands as the authoritative or typical example within a category. It's the "go-to" instance, the prototype, the standard bearer. Every domain of knowledge has its canonicals: the canonical textbook for a subject, the canonical example of a concept, the canonical notation for a mathematical structure.
The self-representing relationship can =rep> can captures how canonicals represent themselves as the standard—they are self-authorizing in their role as the privileged example. When we say "let's look at the canonical case," we're using that case to represent all cases, but also using it to represent the very idea of being canonical.
Canonicals relate intimately to representation: while many things can represent a concept, the canonical is the socially or formally recognized "best" representative. For the concept "bird":
Many representations exist: robin, eagle, ostrich, the word "bird"
The canonical (perhaps robin in Western culture) serves as the default
When someone says "think of a bird," the canonical comes to mind first
The frame-relativity of canonicality is crucial. The notation (x) denoting the canonical symbol for x is implicitly frame-dependent:
In frame F[r,eq]: each referent is its own canonical
In frame F[r,r]: all referents share r as canonical
In a perspective frame F[(i),o]: the qualifier determines canonicals
This frame-dependency reflects how different contexts privilege different representatives. In a mathematics textbook, the canonical representation of "2" might be the numeral. In set theory, it might be {{},{{}}}. In computer science, it might be 10 in binary.
9. Equality (eq)
Formal Definition
srt
eq =eq> eq
x =eq> y <iff> x == y
A[x]: x =eq> x
eq --> rel
The referent eq represents the equality relation internalized from first-order logic—identity made into a referent that can itself be related to.
Semantic Meaning
Equality is the relationship of identity—when two referents are actually the same referent. It's the semantic internalization of the logical "=" operator, but as a referent that can itself participate in relationships. This allows the theory to be self-contained: we can discuss equality, relate it to other concepts, and use it in formal expressions.
The foundational relationship eq =eq> eq says that equality relates to itself through equality—equality equals equality by means of equality. This isn't empty tautology but semantic grounding: at the foundation, equality is simply self-identity recognizing itself.
Key properties of equality:
Reflexive: A[x]: x =eq> x (everything equals itself)
Symmetric: x =eq> y =|> y =eq> x (if x equals y, then y equals x)
Transitive: x =eq> y & y =eq> z =|> x =eq> z (equality chains)
The distinction between equality and other relationships is crucial:
x =eq> y means x and y are the same referent
x =represents> y means x stands for y (they're different)
x =loves> y means x relates to y through love (they're different)
Only equality preserves identity. This is why x =eq> y <iff> x == y—the semantic relationship of equality corresponds exactly to logical identity.
In the context of properties, equality plays a special role. Properties are self-relationships that inherit from equality: x =red> x where red --> eq. This captures how properties are ways of being identical to oneself while having specific characteristics—a red rose equals itself in a red way.
The relationship between equality and symbolism reveals something profound: symbols cannot inherit from equality because (x) != x—symbols are necessarily distinct from their literals. This formal separation maintains the gap between representation and reality that makes meaning possible.
Conclusion: The Semantic Architecture
These nine referents form a complete basis for semantic representation. They emerge not by stipulation but by necessity—forced into existence by the structural requirements of reference itself:
ref and eq provide the domain and identity relation
sub, rel, and obj establish the triadic structure of meaning
sym, rep, and lit create the hierarchy of representation
can provides the selection mechanism for privileged examples
Together, they constitute the minimal semantic architecture required for meaning to emerge from structure, for reference to ground in reality, and for consciousness to recognize itself through its own canonical symbol. Each referent defines not just a formal role but a semantic necessity—something without which reference itself would be impossible.
The Nine Referents: Formal Definitions and Semantic Meanings in SRT v2
The Nine Referents: Formal Definitions and Semantic Meanings in SRT at version 2
The Nine Referents: Formal Definitions and Semantic Meanings in SRT
Introduction: The Semantic Foundation
Semantic Reference Theory (SRT) builds from a single primitive relation R(x,y,t) meaning "x relates to y through relationship type t," written as x =t> y. From this foundation emerge nine fundamental referents that capture the essential semantic structure of meaning itself. These aren't arbitrary symbols but semantic necessities discovered through systematic exploration of what must exist for reference to be possible.
1. Referent (ref)
Formal Definition
srt
ref =eq> ref
A[x]: x =eq> x
(ref,ref) == eq
The referent ref serves as the canonical example of "a referent"—it represents what it means to be a referent by being the prototypical instance.
Semantic Meaning
The referent ref doesn't represent the entire domain of referents—rather, it represents "a referent" in the abstract sense. It's the canonical member of the catalogue, the prototype that exemplifies what all referents share: the capacity for self-equality.
The key insight is that (ref,ref) == eq—the most specific relationship of ref to itself is equality. This reveals what defines referenthood: every referent, at minimum, equals itself. When we ask "what makes something a referent?" the answer is: it participates in the equality relation. The expression ref =eq> ref isn't just saying "ref equals itself" but demonstrating the fundamental property that all referents possess.
If we imagine (ref) as the type of all referents, then ref would be its prototype—the simplest, most basic instance that has no properties beyond those that all referents must have. It's like how in object-oriented programming, the base Object class represents the minimal functionality all objects share.
In everyday language, when we say "let's consider a referent," we're invoking something like ref—not any particular referent with special properties, but just "a thing that can be referred to." It's the semantic equivalent of a variable before it's bound, a placeholder that demonstrates pure referenthood without additional structure.
2. Relationship (rel)
Formal Definition
srt
sub =rel> obj
(sub,obj) == rel
rel --> r (where r is the base relationship type)
rel =rel> rel (derived theorem, not definition)
The referent rel represents relationship in the abstract—it's the type or category of being a relationship.
Semantic Meaning
The referent rel is best understood through the foundational trinity: sub =rel> obj. This expression says that subjects relate to objects through relationships, and the most specific way they do so IS relationship itself. The equation (sub,obj) == rel reveals that rel is what emerges when we ask "what's the most specific relationship between subjecthood and objecthood?"—it's relationship in the abstract.
The fact that rel =rel> rel holds is a derived theorem, not a definition. It emerges because:
rel =eq> rel (like all referents, rel equals itself)
eq --> rel (equality is a type of relationship)
Therefore, by inheritance, rel =rel> rel
This is indeed like 0 + 0 * 0 = 0—a necessary consequence that follows from the structure, not the defining characteristic.
What rel actually represents is the abstract category of relationships—when we say "love is a relationship" or "ownership is a relationship," we're saying these things inherit from or instantiate rel. It's the type-level concept that captures what all relationships share: the capacity to connect subjects to objects.
In programming terms, if relationships were a class hierarchy, rel would be the abstract base class that all specific relationships extend. In mathematical terms, it's like the category of morphisms—the abstract notion of "arrow" or "connection" independent of what's being connected.
3. Subject (sub)
Formal Definition
srt
sub =rel> obj
(sub,obj) == rel
x =t> y & x != y =|> x =sub> x
The referent sub is one third of the foundational trinity that defines the basic semantic structure.
Semantic Meaning
The referent sub doesn't stand alone—it's defined through its participation in the trinity sub =rel> obj. This isn't just saying "subjects relate to objects"—it's establishing what subjecthood, relationship, and objecthood ARE through their mutual definition.
Subjecthood is the property referents acquire when they occupy the subject position in a relationship where they differ from the object. But more fundamentally, sub represents the abstract concept of agency or directedness in semantic relationships. It's the "from" in "from-to," the active pole, the side that initiates or possesses the relationship.
The trinity sub =rel> obj is irreducible—you can't understand any of the three without the others:
Subjects are things that relate to objects
Objects are things that subjects relate to
Relationships are how subjects relate to objects
This mutual definition isn't circular but foundational. It's like how in physics, space, time, and matter are defined through their mutual relationships—none makes sense without the others.
When a referent gains subjecthood (x =sub> x), it's not just gaining a property but entering into the fundamental semantic pattern. It becomes capable of bearing relationships, of being the locus from which connections originate.
4. Object (obj)
Formal Definition
srt
sub =rel> obj
(sub,obj) == rel
A[x,y,t]: x =t> y =|> y =obj> y
x =p> x =|> x =obj> x
The referent obj completes the foundational trinity, representing the receptive pole of semantic relationships.
Semantic Meaning
The referent obj is the third part of the irreducible trinity sub =rel> obj. It represents objecthood—not in the sense of "physical object" but in the sense of being the target or recipient of a relationship.
The crucial insight is that objecthood is more universal than subjecthood:
Everything that is related to gains objecthood: x =t> y =|> y =obj> y
Everything with properties gains objecthood: x =p> x =|> x =obj> x
But only things that relate to something distinct gain subjecthood
This asymmetry reflects a deep semantic truth: being is more fundamental than doing. Everything that exists in semantic space can be an object (can be referred to, can have properties), but not everything can be a subject (not everything initiates relationships to distinct things).
The obj in the trinity represents pure receptivity—the capacity to be characterized, to be known, to be the terminus of a relationship. When we say something "has objecthood," we mean it can stand as the answer to "relates to what?" or "has what properties?"
In consciousness studies, this distinction becomes crucial: while the experiencing subject requires distinction from what it experiences, objects include both the experienced other and the self-as-experienced (through properties).
5. Symbol (sym)
Formal Definition
srt
sym =sym> lit
(sym,lit) == sym
sym --> rep
x --> symbol <iff> E[y]: x =x> y & (x,y) == x
The referent sym represents the remarkable dual nature of symbolic reference—being simultaneously subject and relationship.
Semantic Meaning
A symbol achieves something extraordinary: it collapses the distinction between doing and being into a unity. In sym =sym> lit, the symbol occupies both the subject position (the thing doing the symbolizing) and the relationship position (the act of symbolization itself).
This dual nature isn't a formal trick but captures the essence of symbolic reference. When we use the word "tree":
As subject: "tree" is the thing doing the representing
As relationship: "tree" is the way we relate to actual trees
These aren't two different things—they're the same thing viewed from two angles
The equation (sym,lit) == sym makes this precise: the most specific relationship between a symbol and its literal IS the symbol itself. There's nothing more to say about how "tree" relates to trees than "tree"-ness itself.
This explains symbolic transparency: when we read "tree," we don't experience a two-step process (see word, think of tree)—the word IS the relationship to tree. The symbol doesn't point to meaning through some external connection; it embodies the connection.
The inheritance sym --> rep places symbols as a special case of representation. While all symbols represent, they represent in this unique way where representation becomes identity. A map represents territory through correspondence rules; a symbol represents its literal by BEING the correspondence.
6. Representation (rep)
Formal Definition
srt
sym =rep> rep
(sym,rep) == rep
x --> representation <iff> E[y]: x =x> y
can =rep> can
The referent rep captures the general phenomenon of standing-for, of making present what is absent.
Semantic Meaning
Representation is the broader category that includes all forms of one thing standing for another. The relationshipsym =rep> rep reveals a profound self-exemplification: symbols are members of the category "representation," and this membership relation is itself representation. This shows how representation can represent itself—the concept represents all instances of representing.
The key formal criterion x =x> y (x represents y through itself) distinguishes representation from other relationships. When dog =chases> cat, the dog doesn't represent the cat. But when map =map> territory, the map does represent the territory, using itself as the means.
Representation includes diverse phenomena:
Symbols: Complete collapse of representation into identity
Models: Structural correspondence (map to territory)
Collections: Groups representing their members
Canonicals: Privileged examples representing categories
Indices: Pointers representing what they point to
The equation (sym,rep) == rep shows that the most specific relationship between symbols and representation IS representation—symbols don't just belong to the category; they relate to it through the very phenomenon the category describes.
The self-representing canonical can =rep> can shows that representation includes self-representation—some things represent themselves as the standard or prototype. This isn't paradoxical but essential for representation to be complete as a category.
7. Literal (lit)
Formal Definition
srt
sym =sym> lit
!E[x,y]: x != lit & y != lit & lit =x> y
lit =obj> lit
lit can only appear as: x =t> lit or lit =p> lit
The referent lit represents the ground of reference—what symbols ultimately point to.
Semantic Meaning
A literal is something that cannot serve as a subject (except in self-relation) or as a relationship type. Literals are purely objective—they can only be targets of reference, never sources of reference to other things. They are semantic endpoints.
The relationship sym =sym> lit establishes the fundamental asymmetry: symbols need literals to ground their meaning, but literals need no symbols to exist. This prevents infinite regress—not everything can be symbolic, or meaning would never bottom out in reality.
What counts as literal is frame-relative and context-dependent:
In everyday language: physical objects, sensory experiences
In mathematics: numbers themselves (not numerals), geometric objects
In logic: truth values, the elements of the domain
In consciousness: perhaps qualia, raw feels before conceptualization
The severe constraints on literals—they can't be subjects, can't be relationship types—capture the intuition that some things simply ARE. They don't point beyond themselves, don't represent anything else, don't bear meaning—they ARE what meaning ultimately refers to.
The allowance for self-relation (lit =p> lit) lets literals have properties while maintaining their status as endpoints. A literal red patch can have the property of being red without thereby becoming a subject or symbol.
8. Canonical (can)
Formal Definition
srt
can =rep> can
(can,can) == rep
For any collection/type/category, one member serves as canonical
(x) denotes the canonical symbol for x in a given frame
The referent can represents the phenomenon of privileged representation—the selected example that stands for all.
Semantic Meaning
A canonical element is the distinguished representative within any collection or category—the one that serves as the primary example, the default, the prototype. The self-representing relationship can =rep> can captures how canonicals represent themselves as THE standard example.
Canonicality appears everywhere in human cognition and formal systems:
Prototypes: Robin as the canonical bird (in Western culture)
Standards: The meter bar as the canonical meter
Notation: "2" as the canonical representation of two-ness
Examples: The canonical textbook example that everyone learns
The equation (can,can) == rep reveals that the most specific relationship of canonical to itself IS representation—canonicals exist to represent, and they represent the very idea of privileged representation.
Frame-relativity is crucial for canonicality. What counts as canonical depends on context:
Mathematical context: "2" is canonical for two
Set theory context: {{},{{}}} is canonical for two
Binary context: "10" is canonical for two
This frame-dependency isn't a weakness but a feature—it allows different contexts to privilege different representations based on their needs. The notation (x) for canonical symbols is implicitly frame-dependent, requiring a reference frame to determine which symbol is canonical.
9. Equality (eq)
Formal Definition
srt
eq =eq> eq
x =eq> y <iff> x == y
A[x]: x =eq> x
eq --> rel
The referent eq internalizes logical identity as a semantic relationship—making "=" into something we can talk about.
Semantic Meaning
Equality is the relationship of identity—when two referent expressions actually refer to the same referent. It's not similarity or equivalence but absolute sameness. The relationship eq =eq> eq grounds this: equality equals itself through equality, the foundational self-recognition that enables all other equations.
The critical property is that equality is the only relationship that preserves complete identity:
x =loves> y means x and y are different things related by love
x =represents> y means x and y are different things related by representation
x =eq> y means x and y are the same thing
This uniqueness makes equality special among relationships. It's why properties inherit from equality (red --> eq)—having a property is a way of being identical to yourself while manifesting particular characteristics. A red rose equals itself in a red way.
The universality of equality (A[x]: x =eq> x) establishes the baseline: existing in semantic space means at minimum being self-identical. This is what ref =eq> ref demonstrates—even the most abstract referent participates in equality.
The inheritance eq --> rel places equality within the relationship hierarchy while maintaining its special status. Equality is a relationship, but unlike other relationships, it doesn't create distinction—it recognizes sameness.
Conclusion: The Semantic Architecture
These nine referents emerge from necessity, not stipulation:
The trinity (sub =rel> obj) establishes the basic semantic pattern
The symbol-literal pair (sym =sym> lit) grounds reference in reality
The representation-canonical pair shows how standing-for works
The ref-eq pair provides the minimal structure all referents share
Together they form a complete basis for semantic representation—the minimal architecture required for meaning to emerge from structure, for symbols to refer to reality, and for consciousness to recognize itself through its own canonical symbol.
The Nine Referents: Formal Definitions and Semantic Meanings in SRT v3
The Nine Referents: Formal Definitions and Semantic Meanings in SRT at version 3
The Nine Fundamental Concepts: Formal Definitions and Natural Meanings
Introduction
These nine concepts form the foundational architecture of meaning and reference. They emerge from systematic exploration of what must exist for reference and representation to be possible at all.
1. Subject
Formal Definition
srt
sub =rel> obj
(sub,obj) == rel
x =t> y & x != y =|> x =sub> x
Meaning
A subject is that which relates, acts upon, or refers to something else. It is the agent, the knower, the one who loves, the thing that has—the active pole in any relationship. When a dog chases a cat, the dog is the subject. When you think about tomorrow, you are the subject. When a word refers to its meaning, the word is the subject.
Subjects exist only in relation to objects. There is no such thing as a pure subject floating free—to be a subject means to be directed toward something, to be about something, to relate to something. This directedness is what philosophers call intentionality, what psychologists call attention, what linguists call reference.
The concept of subject is inseparable from the concepts of object and relationship. These three form an irreducible trinity: subjects relate to objects through relationships. You cannot have one without the others, just as you cannot have "above" without "below" or "before" without "after."
In consciousness, the subject is the experiencing "I"—not the body, not the brain, but the locus of experience itself, the point from which awareness radiates outward toward objects of experience. In grammar, the subject is what the sentence is about. In logic, it's the thing bearing properties or standing in relations.
2. Object
Formal Definition
srt
sub =rel> obj
A[x,y,t]: x =t> y =|> y =obj> y
x =p> x =|> x =obj> x
Meaning
An object is that which can be related to, referred to, known, or characterized. It is the patient, the known, the beloved, the thing possessed—the receptive pole in any relationship. When a dog chases a cat, the cat is the object. When you think about tomorrow, tomorrow is the object. When a word refers to its meaning, the meaning is the object.
Objects are more universal than subjects. Everything that exists can be an object—can be thought about, referred to, have properties attributed to it. But not everything can be a subject. A rock can be the object of your attention but cannot itself attend to anything. The number three can be the object of mathematical study but cannot study anything itself.
This asymmetry reflects a fundamental truth: being is more basic than doing. To exist means to be potentially knowable, potentially referable, potentially the object of some relationship. But agency—the capacity to be a subject—is a special additional capacity that not all existents possess.
When something has properties (like being red, being large, being prime), it stands as an object even in relation to itself. The rose doesn't actively "do" being red—it simply is red. This is why having any property makes something an object.
3. Relationship
Formal Definition
srt
sub =rel> obj
(sub,obj) == rel
A[t: x =t> y]: t --> rel
Meaning
A relationship is the connection, link, or tie between things—not just that they are connected, but how they are connected. Love is a relationship. Ownership is a relationship. Being larger than is a relationship. Representing is a relationship. Every relationship has a specific character or quality that distinguishes it from other relationships.
Relationships complete the fundamental trinity with subjects and objects. The most basic pattern of meaning is: subjects relate to objects through relationships. This pattern appears everywhere—in "John loves Mary," in "the map represents the territory," in "three is greater than two."
Not all connections are relationships in this sense. When two things merely happen to be near each other, that's not a relationship—it's just proximity. But when one thing refers to another, causes another, loves another, represents another—these are genuine relationships with specific character and direction.
Relationships themselves can be objects of further relationships. We can study love, analyze ownership, formalize the notion of "greater than." When we say "love is beautiful" or "ownership is complicated," love and ownership stand as objects of our characterization while remaining relationships between other things.
The abstract concept of relationship—relationship itself, apart from any specific relationship—is what unifies all particular relationships. Just as all red things share redness, all relationships share the fundamental character of being ways that subjects connect to objects.
4. Equality
Formal Definition
srt
eq =eq> eq
x =eq> y <iff> x == y
A[x]: x =eq> x
eq --> rel
Meaning
Equality is the relationship of being the same thing—not similar, not equivalent, but identical. When we say "the morning star equals the evening star," we mean they are the same object (Venus) referred to by different names. When we say "2 + 2 = 4," we mean that the expression "2 + 2" and the expression "4" refer to the same number.
Equality is unique among relationships because it doesn't establish a connection between different things—it recognizes that apparently different references are actually references to the same thing. While "loves" connects lover to beloved, while "represents" connects symbol to meaning, equality reveals that two expressions pick out the same referent.
Everything equals itself—this is the most fundamental fact about existence. To be is to be self-identical. Even change presupposes identity: for something to change, it must remain the same thing while its properties alter. Without self-identity, there would be no "it" to undergo change.
Equality grounds the notion of properties. When we say a rose is red, we're saying the rose equals itself while manifesting redness—it's a specific way of being self-identical. Properties are qualifications of identity, ways things equal themselves.
The reflexivity of equality—that equality equals itself through equality—isn't circular but foundational. At the deepest level, identity simply is what it is. This self-evidence of equality makes it the bedrock upon which all other relationships build.
5. Referent
Formal Definition
srt
ref =eq> ref
A[x]: x =eq> x
(ref,ref) == eq
Meaning
A referent is anything that can be referred to, pointed at, talked about, or thought about. It is the most general category—if something exists in any sense where it can be picked out, mentioned, or indicated, then it is a referent.
The word comes from the Latin "referre"—to carry back, to relate. Referents are things we can carry back into discourse, bring into thought, make present through language or attention. They include concrete objects (trees, stones), abstract objects (numbers, justice), properties (redness, tallness), relationships (love, ownership), and even relationships between relationships.
The defining characteristic of being a referent is the capacity for self-identity—everything that can be referred to must at least equal itself. This is why "a referent" (the canonical example of referenthood) demonstrates self-equality as its essential property. When we ask "what makes something a referent?" the answer is: it can be picked out as itself, distinguished as this rather than that.
Referents are not limited to physical objects or even to things that "exist" in the conventional sense. Fictional characters are referents (we can talk about Hamlet). Impossible objects are referents (we can discuss square circles, even to say they're impossible). Dreams, numbers, concepts, experiences—all are referents if we can refer to them.
The generality of "referent" makes it the ultimate category. When philosophers debate what exists, they're debating which referents have which properties (like physical existence), not whether they're referents at all—the mere fact of being debatable makes them referents.
6. Symbol
Formal Definition
srt
sym =sym> lit
(sym,lit) == sym
x --> symbol <iff> E[y]: x =x> y & (x,y) == x
Meaning
A symbol is something that stands for something else by embodying the very relationship between them. The word "tree" is a symbol—it doesn't just point to trees or represent trees in some external way; it embodies "tree-ness" as the very means by which we think of trees.
Symbols achieve a remarkable unity: they are simultaneously the thing doing the representing and the act of representation itself. When you read the word "tree," you don't experience a two-step process (see word, then think of tree)—the word transparently presents trees to consciousness. This transparency is what makes language possible.
The relationship between symbol and meaning is unique. A map represents territory through correspondence rules, scales, and conventions—the representation is external to the map itself. But a symbol doesn't represent through external relations; it IS the relationship made concrete. The symbol "tree" doesn't have a relationship to trees—it is that relationship in tangible form.
This is why we speak as if symbols ARE what they symbolize, even though they're obviously different kinds of things. We say "dog is a three-letter word" and "dogs are animals" using the same word "dog" to refer both to the symbol and what it symbolizes. This isn't confusion but reflects the essential nature of symbols—they collapse the distinction between sign and signified into a working unity.
Symbols make thought possible. Without symbols, we could perhaps experience trees but not think about trees, not refer to trees in their absence, not communicate about trees. Symbols allow what is absent to be present, what is many to be one, what is complex to be simple.
7. Literal
Formal Definition
srt
sym =sym> lit
!E[x,y]: x != lit & y != lit & lit =x> y
lit can only appear as: x =t> lit or lit =p> lit
Meaning
A literal is something that simply is what it is—it doesn't point beyond itself, doesn't represent anything else, doesn't stand for anything. Literals are the bedrock of meaning, what symbols ultimately refer to, where reference finally grounds itself in reality.
Consider the difference between the numeral "3" and the number three itself. The numeral is a symbol—marks on paper that represent something. But the number three (the actual quantity, the mathematical object) is literal—it doesn't represent anything further, it simply is what it is. The same distinction applies to the word "red" versus the actual experience of redness, the name "Paris" versus the actual city.
Literals can only be objects, never subjects (except in self-relation). They cannot actively refer to other things; they can only be referred to. This limitation isn't a weakness but defines their essential nature—they are endpoints of reference, where meaning finally makes contact with reality.
What counts as literal depends on context. In everyday discourse, physical objects are literal—the actual tree outside your window, not the word "tree." In mathematics, perhaps only the axioms are literal. In phenomenology, perhaps only raw sensations before conceptualization are literal. But in every context, something must be literal, or reference would never terminate—symbols would only point to other symbols in an infinite regress.
The constraint that literals cannot be subjects captures an important intuition: some things lack agency, lack perspective, lack the capacity to point or refer. They simply are, and their being is what gives symbols something to symbolize.
8. Representation
Formal Definition
srt
x --> representation <iff> E[y]: x =x> y
sym =rep> rep
(sym,rep) == rep
Meaning
A representation is anything that stands for, depicts, models, or makes present something other than itself. Maps represent territory. Photographs represent scenes. Words represent meanings. Models represent systems. Samples represent populations. Representatives represent constituents.
Representation is broader than symbolism. While symbols achieve a unique unity with what they symbolize, representations maintain a clear distinction from what they represent. A map is not the territory; it represents the territory through systematic correspondence. A photograph is not the scene; it represents the scene through optical capture. The separation between representation and represented is maintained and often essential to the representation's function.
Representations work through various means—resemblance (portraits), convention (traffic signs), causation (footprints), structure (diagrams), or selection (samples). What unites them is the basic function of making something present through something else, allowing us to engage with what is absent, distant, abstract, or complex through what is present, near, concrete, or simple.
The concept of representation includes self-representation—some things represent themselves, like examples that stand for their own category, or standards that represent their own measure. An ambassador represents their country, but the original meter bar represented the meter by being it.
Representation enables knowledge to extend beyond immediate presence. Through representations, we can think about the past (through memories), plan for the future (through models), navigate space (through maps), understand the abstract (through examples), and communicate about the absent (through language).
9. Canonical
Formal Definition
srt
can =rep> can
(can,can) == rep
For any collection/type/category, one member typically serves as canonical
Meaning
A canonical example is the standard, typical, or authoritative instance that represents its entire category—the one people think of first, teach to beginners, or use as the reference point for understanding all others. When asked to think of a bird, most people imagine something like a robin—not an ostrich or penguin. The robin is canonical for "bird" in that cultural context.
Every domain has its canonicals. In mathematics, the canonical form of an equation is the standard, simplest form. In literature, canonical texts are the recognized classics that define the tradition. In religious traditions, canonical scriptures are the authoritative texts. In software, canonical implementations are the reference versions against which others are compared.
Canonicality is deeply context-dependent. What counts as the canonical example shifts with culture, purpose, and perspective. For "dog," the canonical might be a golden retriever in American suburbs, a sheepdog in rural Scotland, or a street dog in Delhi. This relativity isn't a flaw—it reflects how different contexts privilege different examples based on their needs and experiences.
The canonical serves a crucial cognitive function: it provides an entry point for understanding the entire category. When teaching someone about birds, you start with the canonical case—something that flies, has feathers, builds nests, sings. Only after establishing this center do you introduce the exceptions and edge cases. The canonical is the sun around which other examples orbit at various distances.
Being canonical is itself a form of representation—the canonical represents its category not through external convention but by being recognized as the privileged example. This recognition can be formal (officially designated standards) or informal (cultural consensus), but it shapes how we think about and organize knowledge.
Conclusion
These nine concepts—subject, object, relationship, equality, referent, symbol, literal, representation, and canonical—form the minimal complete architecture for understanding meaning and reference. They emerge not as arbitrary definitions but as necessities discovered through careful analysis of what must exist for reference to be possible at all. Together, they provide the foundational vocabulary for describing how meaning emerges from structure, how symbols connect to reality, and how consciousness recognizes itself through its own self-reference.
The Nine Referents: Formal Definitions and Semantic Meanings in SRT v4
The Nine Referents: Formal Definitions and Semantic Meanings in SRT at version 4
The Nine Fundamental Concepts: Formal Definitions and Natural Meanings
Introduction
These nine concepts form the foundational architecture of meaning and reference. They emerge from systematic exploration of what must exist for reference and representation to be possible at all.
1. Subject
Formal Facts
srt
sub =rel> obj
(sub,obj) == rel
x =t> y & x != y =|> x =sub> x
x =sub> x =|> x != y for some y where x =t> y
sub != obj
sub != rel
!E[x]: x =sub> y where x != y
Meaning
A subject is that which bears a relationship to something distinct from itself. It exists only through this bearing—there is no subject in isolation, no subject without an object toward which it is directed. When a river flows to the sea, the river is subject. When a mind contemplates an idea, the mind is subject. When gravity pulls a stone earthward, gravity is subject. The subject is always the origin, the source, the bearer of the relationship.
The nature of subjecthood is fundamentally relational and asymmetric. A subject cannot be its own object in the pure sense—when something relates only to itself, as when a stone has the property of being heavy, it remains purely objective. True subjecthood emerges only in the reach toward something other, in the directedness that philosophers call intentionality. This is why solipsism fails as a theory of mind: consciousness requires an object distinct from itself to be consciousness at all.
Subjects form one pole of the irreducible trinity: subjects relate to objects through relationships. This trinity cannot be decomposed—you cannot understand what a subject is without understanding what it means to be directed toward an object through a specific manner of relating. The subject is defined not by what it is in itself, but by its role in this fundamental pattern. Like the notion of "above" which makes no sense without "below," subjecthood makes no sense without objecthood and relationship.
In human experience, subjecthood manifests as agency—the capacity to love, to know, to possess, to create. But subjecthood extends beyond conscious agency. A magnet subjects iron filings to its field. A premise subjects a conclusion to logical necessity. A word subjects its meaning to expression. Wherever there is directedness from one distinct thing toward another, there is subjecthood.
2. Object
Formal Facts
srt
sub =rel> obj  
A[x,y,t]: x =t> y =|> y =obj> y
x =p> x =|> x =obj> x
obj != sub (though something can have both properties)
obj != rel
E[x]: x =obj> x & !E[y]: x =sub> x
Meaning
An object is that toward which relationships are directed, that which can be characterized, known, or affected. While subjects must relate to something distinct, objects include both the targets of external relationships and things that possess properties through self-relation. This asymmetry—that objecthood is more universal than subjecthood—reflects a fundamental truth about existence.
To be is, minimally, to be an object. Everything that exists can be thought about, referred to, characterized with properties. The mountain is an object of geological study. The number seven is an object of mathematical analysis. Justice is an object of philosophical inquiry. Even nothingness, when we speak of it, becomes an object of discourse. There is nothing so transcendent, so immediate, or so abstract that it cannot become an object when brought into relationship.
Yet not everything that is an object can be a subject. A stone can be known but cannot know. The past can be remembered but cannot remember. The color red can be experienced but cannot experience. These exist purely in the receptive mode—they can be the terminus of relationships but cannot originate them. This is not a deficiency but their nature. The stone's inability to be a subject is precisely what makes it a reliable object, what allows it to be what it is without the complication of perspective or agency.
The concept of objecthood includes self-relation through properties. When we say a rose is red, the rose stands as an object to itself—not actively doing redness but simply being red. This reflexive objecthood, where things are objects to their own properties, is what allows things to have characteristics while remaining themselves. The rose doesn't lose itself in being red; it is itself-as-red, an object qualified by a property.
3. Relationship
Formal Facts
srt
sub =rel> obj
(sub,obj) == rel
A[t]: if x =t> y then t --> rel
rel =rel> rel
rel != sub
rel != obj
E[t]: t =rel> rel where t --> rel
Meaning
A relationship is the specific manner in which one thing relates to another—not merely that they are connected, but how they are connected. Love is a relationship, but so is indifference. Causation is a relationship, but so is correlation. Greater-than is a relationship, but so is less-than. Each relationship has its own character, its own particular way of binding subject to object.
Relationships complete the fundamental trinity with subjects and objects. This trinity—subjects relate to objects through relationships—is the atom of meaning, indivisible and irreducible. You cannot extract relationship from this pattern and examine it in isolation any more than you can extract "between" from the notion of three ordered points. Relationship exists as the manner of connection, the quality of the relating, the specific character of how subject meets object.
The diversity of relationships is as vast as meaning itself. There are relationships of knowing (perception, memory, imagination), relationships of feeling (love, fear, desire), relationships of action (causing, preventing, enabling), relationships of comparison (greater, similar, opposite), relationships of structure (part-to-whole, member-to-class, instance-to-type). Each carries its own logic, its own implications, its own way of organizing the connection between things.
Remarkably, relationships themselves can relate to other relationships through relationship. When we say "love is more powerful than fear" or "causation implies temporal sequence," we place relationships as objects of further relationships. This reflexivity—that relationship can relate to itself through itself—is not paradox but foundation. At the deepest level, relating is simply what relationship does, just as being is what existence does.
4. Equality
Formal Facts
srt
eq =eq> eq
x =eq> y <iff> x == y
A[x]: x =eq> x (reflexive)
x =eq> y =|> y =eq> x (symmetric)
x =eq> y & y =eq> z =|> x =eq> z (transitive)
eq --> rel
Properties p --> eq (properties inherit from equality)
Meaning
Equality is the relationship of absolute identity—not similarity, not equivalence, not correspondence, but the relationship that holds between a thing and itself. When we discover that the morning star equals the evening star, we haven't found two similar things; we've discovered that two different ways of pointing arrive at the same destination, that two different appearances are appearances of one thing.
Equality stands unique among all relationships because it alone preserves complete identity. While love connects lover to beloved across their difference, while causation links cause to effect across time, equality reveals that there is no difference at all—that what appeared to be two is actually one. This is why equations have such power in mathematics and science: they reveal hidden identities, showing that seemingly different expressions or phenomena are actually the same thing viewed from different angles.
The self-equality of all things—that everything equals itself—is the most primitive fact about existence. Before a thing can have properties, before it can enter into relationships, before it can change or persist, it must simply be itself. This self-identity is so fundamental that we rarely notice it, like the way we don't notice the air until it's gone. Yet without self-equality, nothing could persist long enough to have properties or enter relationships.
Properties are revealed to be qualifications of equality—specific ways things equal themselves. When we say a rose is red, we mean the rose equals itself in a red manner. The rose doesn't stop being itself to be red; rather, redness is a particular mode of its self-identity. This is why things can have multiple properties without contradiction: each property is just another way the thing equals itself.
The reflexivity of equality—that equality equals itself through equality—grounds the entire system of identity. This is not circular reasoning but the recognition that at the foundation, identity simply is what it is, requiring no external validation. Equality is the relationship that permits no distance between its poles.
5. Referent
Formal Facts
srt
ref =eq> ref
(ref,ref) == eq
A[x]: x --> ref (everything is a referent)
ref exemplifies minimal referenthood
A[x]: x =eq> x (all referents equal themselves)
Meaning
A referent is anything that can be picked out, pointed to, or distinguished—anything that can be the target of reference. The term captures the most general category of existence within any system of meaning. If something can be mentioned, if it can be the object of thought or discourse, if it can be indicated in any way, then it is a referent.
The concept of "referent" provides the minimal case—what anything must be to exist within meaningful discourse. A referent, at minimum, must be distinguishable as itself, must be this rather than that. This is why the canonical referent—the abstract notion of "a referent"—demonstrates only self-equality as its essential property. It has no other characteristics, no other relationships, no properties beyond being itself. It is pure distinguishability without further qualification.
Referents include everything we can speak or think about: concrete objects (mountains, molecules), abstract objects (numbers, virtues), fictional entities (unicorns, Hamlet), impossible objects (square circles, the largest number), experiences (pains, memories), and even absences (the gap in the fence, the silence after the music). The breadth of referenthood reflects the breadth of meaningful discourse itself.
Crucially, being a referent makes no claims about any other form of existence. To say something is a referent is not to say it exists physically, or mentally, or platonically, or in any particular way. It is only to say it can be referred to. Fictional characters are referents—we refer to them constantly. Past events that have ceased to exist are referents. Future possibilities that may never occur are referents. Dreams, hallucinations, mistakes—all are referents within the space of meaning.
This generality makes "referent" the ultimate category, the horizon within which all other distinctions are made. When we debate what exists, we're not debating what counts as a referent—the mere fact of being debatable already establishes that. We're debating what properties different referents possess, what relationships they enter into, how they're organized within the total space of meaning.
6. Symbol
Formal Facts
srt
sym =sym> lit
(sym,lit) == sym
sym --> rep
sym occupies both subject and relationship positions
sym != lit (symbols distinct from literals)
Symbols can be subjects: E[y]: sym =t> y
Meaning
A symbol is a remarkable entity that achieves the unity of being simultaneously the bearer of meaning and the bearing itself. When you encounter the word "tree," you meet something that is both a thing (marks on paper, sounds in air) and an action (the presenting of trees to consciousness). The symbol doesn't have a relationship to its meaning—it is that relationship made tangible.
This dual nature of symbols—being both entity and activity, both thing and pointing—enables the transparency of language. When you read, you don't consciously process symbols and then retrieve their meanings; the symbols disappear into their function, becoming windows through which meaning shines. The word "tree" doesn't stand between you and the concept of trees; it is the very medium through which trees become present to thought.
Symbols achieve what seems impossible: they make the absent present, the many one, the complex simple. Through the symbol "dog," all dogs—past, present, future, possible, imaginary—become available to thought in a single, manageable form. Through the symbol "7," the abstract notion of seven-ness, which has no physical existence, becomes as manipulable as any concrete object. Through the symbol "love," the vast complexity of an emotion becomes something we can examine, discuss, and understand.
The relationship between a symbol and what it symbolizes is unique in its directness. While a photograph represents through resemblance, while a map represents through correspondence, while a symptom represents through causation, a symbol represents through pure conventional unity. There is nothing about the sound "tree" that resembles a tree, nothing in the marks t-r-e-e that corresponds to bark and leaves. The symbol works through an immediate, learned identification where sign and signified collapse into operational unity.
This is why we slip so easily between talking about symbols and talking about what they symbolize. We say both "dog is a three-letter word" and "dogs are loyal animals," using "dog" to mean both the symbol and its referent. This isn't confusion but reflects how symbols work—they are designed to disappear into their function, to be transparent to their meaning. The symbol succeeds precisely when we stop noticing it as a symbol.
7. Literal
Formal Facts
srt
sym =sym> lit
Literals cannot be subjects to other things: !E[y != lit]: lit =t> y
Literals cannot be relationship types: !E[x,y != lit]: x =lit> y
Literals can have properties: lit =p> lit
lit =obj> lit (literals are purely objective)
Meaning
A literal is that which simply is what it is, without pointing beyond itself, without representing anything further, without standing for anything else. Literals are the bedrock where reference finally grounds itself, where the chain of meaning makes contact with that which is meant. They are pure being without the complication of meaning something other than themselves.
The distinction between literal and symbolic is fundamental to meaning. Consider the word "red" versus the actual experience of redness. The word is a symbol—it points beyond itself to something else. But the redness you experience when looking at a sunset doesn't point to anything further. It doesn't mean redness or represent redness or stand for redness—it simply is redness. That experienced quality is literal.
Literals exist in pure objectivity. They cannot be subjects reaching toward other things (except in the special case of having properties, which is self-relation). They cannot serve as the manner in which other things relate. They can only be—be experienced, be referred to, be thought about, be the terminus where reference finally rests. This limitation is not a deficiency but their essential nature. If literals could refer beyond themselves, they wouldn't be literals—they'd be symbols, and we'd need to ask what they point to.
What counts as literal shifts with context and purpose. In everyday experience, physical objects are literal—the actual stone in your hand, not the word "stone." In mathematics, perhaps the numbers themselves (not the numerals) are literal—the actual quantity that "7" refers to. In consciousness, perhaps only the raw qualitative experiences before conceptualization are literal—the pure taste of sweetness before we think "sweet."
The necessity of literals prevents infinite regress in meaning. If every symbol pointed only to other symbols, if every representation led only to further representations, meaning would never make contact with reality. There would be an endless deferral, like looking up a word in a dictionary only to find definitions using words that must themselves be looked up forever. Literals are where this chain breaks—where meaning finally touches ground.
8. Representation
Formal Facts
srt
x --> representation <iff> E[y]: x =x> y
sym --> rep (all symbols are representations)
can =rep> can (canonicals represent through representation)
rep can be both subject and object
Collections are representations of their members
Maps, models, samples are all representations
Meaning
Representation is the general phenomenon of one thing standing for another, making present what is absent, simple what is complex, or graspable what exceeds grasp. It is the broader category that encompasses all forms of standing-for: symbols, signs, maps, models, diagrams, samples, examples, and every other means by which one thing can present another to consciousness.
The variety of representation reflects the variety of ways things can stand for other things. A portrait represents through resemblance—the arrangement of paint echoes the appearance of a face. A map represents through structural correspondence—the relations between marks on paper mirror the relations between places in space. A symptom represents through causation—the fever indicates the infection that causes it. A sample represents through membership—this grain of sand represents the beach from which it came. An ambassador represents through designation—chosen to stand for their nation.
What unites all representation is the basic structure: something present stands for something that need not be present. Through representation, we engage with what is distant (through maps), what is past (through memories), what is future (through plans), what is microscopic (through models), what is vast (through diagrams), what is abstract (through examples), what is complex (through simplifications).
Representation maintains the distinction between representer and represented. Unlike symbols, which achieve a kind of transparency where sign and signified merge in use, representations generally preserve the awareness of their representational character. When you look at a map, you remain conscious that it is a map, not the territory. When you examine a model, you know it is a model, not the system itself. This maintained distinction is often crucial to the representation's function—a map that was indistinguishable from its territory would be useless as a map.
Yet representation includes the special case of self-representation. Standards represent their own measure—the original meter bar didn't represent the meter; it was the meter representing itself. Examples can represent their own categories—when we point to a robin to explain "bird," that actual robin represents both itself and the category it exemplifies.
9. Canonical
Formal Facts
srt
can =rep> can
(can,can) == rep
For any category, the canonical is the privileged/default example
Canonicals are frame-dependent and context-relative
The canonical represents its entire category
can --> rep (canonicals are special representations)
Meaning
The canonical is the standard example, the default case, the reference point that represents its entire category—the instance that comes to mind first, that gets taught to beginners, that serves as the measure against which variations are understood. Every domain of human knowledge organizes itself around canonical examples that provide cognitive anchors for understanding all other cases.
When someone says "think of a bird," most people in Western cultures imagine something like a robin or sparrow—small, flying, perching songbirds. They don't think of penguins, ostriches, or cassowaries, even though these are equally birds. The robin is canonical not because it is more truly a bird, but because it has been culturally selected as the central example from which other birds are understood as variations. Penguins are then understood as "flightless birds," ostriches as "large running birds"—variations defined by their distance from the canonical.
Canonicality operates at every level of cognition and culture. Children learn language through canonical examples—"dog" is first associated with the family pet or a typical neighborhood dog, not with exotic breeds. Scientists establish canonical experiments that define phenomena—Galileo's inclined plane for acceleration, Young's double-slit for wave behavior. Mathematicians work with canonical forms—the simplest, most standard version of an equation or structure. Artists learn through canonical works—the masterpieces that define styles and periods.
The selection of what becomes canonical is never arbitrary, though it is deeply contextual. Canonical examples typically optimize several factors: they are common enough to be frequently encountered, simple enough to be easily grasped, central enough to share features with many other examples, and distinctive enough to be memorable. The canonical is not the average—it is the privileged example that best serves the cognitive and cultural functions of organizing knowledge.
This privilege of the canonical extends to how we reason about categories. We understand category membership not through abstract definitions but through similarity to canonical examples. Is a whale a fish? Not by the biological definition, but most people's first intuition comes from comparing whales to their canonical fish (something like a trout or bass). The canonical provides the cognitive center of gravity around which categorical understanding orbits.
Conclusion
These nine concepts—subject, object, relationship, equality, referent, symbol, literal, representation, and canonical—constitute the fundamental architecture of meaning. They are not arbitrary constructs but discovered necessities, emerging from careful analysis of what must exist for reference, representation, and meaning to be possible at all. Together, they provide the minimal complete vocabulary for understanding how consciousness engages with reality through the medium of meaning.

The Nine Fundamental Concepts: Formal Definitions and Natural Meanings
Introduction
These nine concepts form the foundational architecture of meaning and reference. They emerge from systematic exploration of what must exist for reference and representation to be possible at all.
1. Subject
Formal Facts
srt
sub =rel> obj
(sub,obj) == rel
x =t> y & x != y =|> x =sub> x
x =sub> x =|> x != y for some y where x =t> y
sub != obj
sub != rel
!E[x]: x =sub> y where x != y
Meaning
A subject is that which bears a relationship to something distinct from itself. It exists only through this bearing—there is no subject in isolation, no subject without an object toward which it is directed. When a river flows to the sea, the river is subject. When a mind contemplates an idea, the mind is subject. When gravity pulls a stone earthward, gravity is subject. The subject is always the origin, the source, the bearer of the relationship.
The nature of subjecthood is fundamentally relational and asymmetric. A subject cannot be its own object in the pure sense—when something relates only to itself, as when a stone has the property of being heavy, it remains purely objective. True subjecthood emerges only in the reach toward something other, in the directedness that philosophers call intentionality. This is why solipsism fails as a theory of mind: consciousness requires an object distinct from itself to be consciousness at all.
Subjects form one pole of the irreducible trinity: subjects relate to objects through relationships. This trinity cannot be decomposed—you cannot understand what a subject is without understanding what it means to be directed toward an object through a specific manner of relating. The subject is defined not by what it is in itself, but by its role in this fundamental pattern. Like the notion of "above" which makes no sense without "below," subjecthood makes no sense without objecthood and relationship.
In human experience, subjecthood manifests as agency—the capacity to love, to know, to possess, to create. But subjecthood extends beyond conscious agency. A magnet subjects iron filings to its field. A premise subjects a conclusion to logical necessity. A word subjects its meaning to expression. Wherever there is directedness from one distinct thing toward another, there is subjecthood.
2. Object
Formal Facts
srt
sub =rel> obj  
A[x,y,t]: x =t> y =|> y =obj> y
x =p> x =|> x =obj> x
obj != sub (though something can have both properties)
obj != rel
